text.p: A smaller than expected first-quarter loss at Coca-Cola Enterprises Inc sent the company's stock soaring on Tuesday, as solid volume trends in the United States and Europe raised expectations for the rest of 1997
The Atlanta-based bottler of Coke products reported a $0.24 per share loss for the first three months of 1997, excluding a $0.03 one-time charge for the redemption of long-term debt.

Although the result contrasted with a $0.04 per share profit a year ago, it came in well ahead of expectations on Wall Street, where the consensus expectation was for a quarterly shortfall of $0.30 a share, according to First Call.
"The results were extremely good," said UBS Securities analyst Anton Brenner.

Coke Enterprises' stock climbed 1-7/8 or 3.4 percent, to 57-1/2 on the New York Stock Exchange as at least two analysts raised their earnings estimates for 1997. The percentage gain outstripped the Dow Jones Industrial Average, which was 99 points or 1.54 percent higher at the time.
UBS' Brenner raised his 1997 estimate by a nickel to $1.05 a share, while predicting stronger sales performances in the United States and Europe for later this year.
First Call said three analysts changed their 1997 numbers. But one lowered an unusually high figure. As a result, the 1997 Street consensus was unchanged at $0.99 a share.

"The company consistently under-promises and over-delivers," said David Goldman of Robinson Humphrey. "They've set 8-9 percent minimum growth in comparable cash operating profit. That is the target in the current year. And it probably means they'll achieve something higher."
Among the strongest indicators in the Coke Enterprises results was a nine percent jump in U.S. case volumes, its best quarterly volume increase in the domestic market since 1988.
Meanwhile, European volumes increased 14 percent for the company, in which Coca-Cola has a 44 percent stake.
Analysts said the U.S. volume rise came despite extreme competition and predicted the pace would be sustained.

They also expressed enthusiasm for the company's coming performance this year in Europe, where it has spent $2.92 billion to purchase Coke bottling operations in Belgium, France and Britain within the past eight months.
In 1996, the European soft-drink market was weakened by bad weather late in the year.

"We've got an indication of how much leverage they could have outside this country, in terms of developing accelerating volume trends in Europe in particular," said Prudential Securities' George Thompson.

"The real benefits are going to come this year in the third and fourth quarter...in the third quarter last year they had seasonably poor weather, and the third quarter's the biggest quarter over there. In the fourth-quarter, you may see similar trends to what we saw in the first-quarter."

In February, Coke Enteprises bought U.K. bottler Coca-Cola and Schweppes Beverages Ltd from joint owners Coca-Cola and Cadbury-Schweppes for $2 billion. Last July, it purchased Coca-Cola bottling operations in Belgium and France for $915 million.

The U.K. purchase had a dilutive effect which helped produce the $0.24 per share first-quarter loss. Other factors included increased noncash Selling, General and Administrative expenses related to activating a stock compensation plan.
Analysts said the loss was smaller than anticipated mainly because SG&A and interest expenses undershot expectations.
